issues.description: The problem statement and UML specify a SealSaloon constructor that takes a String parameter (saloon name), but the provided solution implements a no-argument constructor and the template's example usage also constructs SealSaloon with no arguments. This mismatch can confuse students about the required constructor signature and whether they must store a saloon name.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the constructor requirement consistent across artifacts. Either (A) update the template and solution to implement a constructor SealSaloon(String name) that stores the name in a (private) field and add a getter getName(), and update any instantiation sites (e.g., Main) to pass a String; or (B) revise the problem statement/UML to specify a no-argument constructor. Option A preserves the original textual requirement and eliminates the mismatch.

issues.description: The problem statement's UML and text specify a constructor SealSaloon(String) (a constructor that takes the saloon name), but the template usage and the provided solution implement only a no-argument constructor SealSaloon(). This API/signature mismatch for the same conceptual entity (the SealSaloon constructor) can confuse students: the instructions ask them to implement or use a constructor with a String parameter while the starter code and reference solution do not provide it.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the API consistent: either update the problem statement to require a no-argument constructor, or modify the template and solution to provide a constructor SealSaloon(String name) (and store the name in a private field with a getter). Preferably add a public SealSaloon(String name) constructor to SealSaloon and keep or overload the no-arg constructor so the implementation matches the UML and textual requirement.
